entities.name: Lucius Furius Philus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Furius Philus, a prominent Roman statesman and intellectual, served as consul in 136 BC, playing a pivotal, albeit controversial, role in Rome's diplomatic efforts during the protracted Numantine War in Hispania Citerior. A distinguished member of the influential Scipionic Circle, Philus was celebrated for his oratorical skills and his profound engagement with Greek philosophy, embodying the Hellenization of Roman elite culture in the mid-2nd century BC. His political career intersected with critical moments of Roman expansion and internal debate, particularly concerning military discipline and treaty obligations.

During his consulship, Philus was dispatched to Numantia alongside his consular colleague, Sextus Calpurnius Piso Frugi, tasked with addressing the ongoing military stalemate. His most notable action involved the formal surrender of Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, a previous consul who had signed a humiliating treaty with the Numantines without senatorial approval. Philus, acting under the Senate's decree, delivered Mancinus naked and bound to the Numantines, an act intended to nullify the treaty and restore Roman honor, though the Numantines refused to accept him. This episode underscored Rome's rigid adherence to legalistic principles in foreign policy and its uncompromising stance on perceived breaches of military conduct.
